title: Asymmetric Information
subtitle: Lecture 1 — Why credit markets don't clear like ordinary goods markets
examWeight: Core. On every recent paper. FINAL: May 2025 Q3 (20 pts adverse-selection vs moral-hazard essay), Final 2023 Q3, Final 2022 Q2 (Akerlof-style numerical). MID-TERM precedent: Feb 2025 Q1+Q4 (covenants, T/F).

sections.heading: The two information problems
sections.body:
**Adverse selection (pre-contract / ex-ante).** The lender cannot tell good borrowers from bad ones. With pooled pricing, low-risk borrowers — who would be over-charged — exit the market, leaving the lender with a worse-than-average pool. Akerlof's lemons problem: high quality is driven out by low quality.

**Moral hazard (post-contract / ex-post).** After funds are disbursed, the borrower may take on more risk than promised. The borrower captures the upside; the lender bears the downside. Without monitoring, this is the lender's problem, not the borrower's.

Both problems are about information asymmetries between contracting parties — and both can persist in equilibrium because the informed party cannot credibly commit to behave well, and the uninformed party cannot perfectly verify.

sections.heading: Akerlof's Lemons model — the formal setup
sections.body:
The textbook example used in Lecture 1 (Greenbaum & Thakor ch. 1, p. 10–15). Three quality classes of cars exist:

• **q1** — best quality, market value **$10**, breakdown probability **0.1**
• **q2** — middle quality, market value **$5**, breakdown probability **0.5**
• **q3** — lemons, market value **$0**, breakdown probability **1.0** (always break)

Sellers know their car's quality; buyers know only the distribution.

**Without warranties — the unravelling.** Buyers offer a pooled price reflecting average expected quality. Owners of q1 cars refuse to sell at that pooled price (they know their car is worth more), so they exit. Buyers update — pooled price falls. Now q2 owners exit. Only q3 (lemons) remain trading. **Asymmetric information drives high quality out of the market.**

**With warranties — separating equilibrium.** A q1 seller can credibly signal quality by offering a warranty whose expected cost is low (because q1 rarely breaks). The warranty terms must satisfy an **Incentive Compatibility (IC) condition** so that q2 sellers cannot profitably mimic q1 by offering the same warranty: a q2 seller's expected payoff under the q1 warranty (which factors in the higher likelihood of having to pay out) must be ≤ their truthful payoff. By convention, indifference is treated as truth-telling, and the IC condition is solved as an equality.

**Non-dissipative vs dissipative signals.**
• A **non-dissipative** signal transfers cost from one party to another — a warranty payout flows from seller to buyer. Total surplus is preserved.
• A **dissipative** signal destroys surplus — e.g. burning resources or paying repair costs that nobody captures.

Warranties are typically non-dissipative — and that is why they work as an efficient separating mechanism.

**Application to credit markets.** Replace cars with borrowers and quality with creditworthiness. A bank that offers a single uniform interest rate is the equivalent of a buyer offering a pooled price. Safe borrowers exit (over-charged); risky borrowers stay (under-charged); the loan portfolio adversely selects toward the worst risks. Mitigants — collateral, covenants, signalling, screening — are the credit-market analogues of the used-car warranty.

sections.heading: Stiglitz–Weiss credit rationing
sections.body:
Raising the loan rate has two adverse effects:

• It worsens the borrower pool — only riskier types accept (adverse selection).
• It incentivises riskier project choice — borrowers who already have a high cost of borrowing pick high-variance projects (moral hazard).

Both effects can offset the direct revenue gain from a higher rate. The bank's expected profit becomes a non-monotonic function of the loan rate, peaking at some r* below the market-clearing rate. The bank optimally sets r* and **rations credit** at that rate — denying loans to some applicants rather than charging them more. Credit markets do not clear through price like grain markets do.

sections.heading: Mitigants
sections.body:
**Adverse selection (screening, ex-ante):**
• Credit-scoring models that aggregate income, debt, repayment history into a quantitative risk measure.
• Financial-statement analysis for corporate borrowers.
• Risk-based pricing: differentiate rates by individual quality rather than offer pooled terms.
• Relationship banking: long-run relationships reveal private information.

**Moral hazard (monitoring, ex-post):**
• Loan covenants — affirmative (require certain actions) and negative (prohibit certain actions). Examples: minimum equity ratio, dividend restrictions, debt limits, FCF use restrictions.
• Post-disbursement monitoring: regular reporting, site visits, financial reviews.
• Waiver discipline: when covenants are breached, banks can renegotiate or accelerate.

**Both:**
• **Collateral.** Pledged collateral signals borrower commitment (mitigates adverse selection — risky borrowers less willing to pledge personal assets) AND provides skin in the game post-disbursement (mitigates moral hazard).

sections.heading: Worked exam pattern
sections.body: Almost every year asks: **(a) define asymmetric information, explain adverse selection vs moral hazard, (b) give examples of mitigants for each.** The May 2025 final (Q3, 20 pts) used exactly this template. Memorise: pre/post distinction, two-mitigant categories (screening + monitoring), collateral as the both-purposes signal.

title: Qualitative Asset Transformation
subtitle: Lecture 2 — Bank functions, FI taxonomy, and the source of bank fragility
examWeight: Core. FINAL: May 2025 Q2 (15 pts — define + societal good + risks/management). Recurring framing for liquidity-risk and bank-model questions on every paper.

sections.heading: The five dimensions of transformation
sections.body:
Banks transform the attributes of financial claims along five dimensions:

• **Duration / term-to-maturity** — long mortgages funded by short deposits.
• **Divisibility / unit size** — large corporate loans funded by many small deposits.
• **Liquidity** — illiquid assets funded by liquid liabilities.
• **Credit risk** — risky assets transformed into safer (insured) deposits.
• **Numeraire / currency** — foreign assets funded by domestic-currency liabilities.

QAT is what banks fundamentally DO. It's the source of their economic value (they meet customer needs that the client could not directly access), and it's the source of their fragility (every transformation creates a mismatch that exposes the bank to a corresponding risk).

sections.heading: Societal benefits
sections.body:
• **Economic growth** — channels short-term savings into long-term investment.
• **Liquidity provision** — savers stay liquid; borrowers get long maturities.
• **Risk-sharing and diversification** — savers gain access to professionally-monitored, diversified credit exposure.
• **Information production** — delegated monitoring economises on duplicated screening costs.

Without QAT, savers and borrowers would have to match directly on duration, size, liquidity, risk and currency — a near-impossible coordination problem.

sections.heading: Risks created and how they are managed
sections.body:
**Risks:**
• **Liquidity / funding risk** — long assets cannot be liquidated quickly; short funding might dry up.
• **Credit risk** — exposure to borrower default on long-term assets.
• **Interest-rate risk** — yield-curve flattening or inversion turns the carry negative; rate spikes hit asset values and funding cost simultaneously.
• **Currency risk** — when asset and liability currencies differ.

**Bank-level management:**
• Liquidity reserves (HQLA) and Asset-Liability Management.
• Credit-scoring, diversification, covenants.
• Interest-rate swaps, FX hedges.

**Society-level management:**
• Lender of last resort (Bagehot's rule) — central bank lends to solvent banks against good collateral.
• Capital requirements (Basel III) for unexpected loss.
• Liquidity rules (LCR ≥ 100%, NSFR ≥ 100%).
• Deposit insurance to prevent self-fulfilling runs.
• Resolution framework (BRRD bail-in) to handle failure without taxpayer cost.

The **central bank as LOLR** is the keystone — without it, fractional-reserve banking would not be viable.

sections.heading: Key insight: every transformation has a cost
sections.body:
There is no free lunch. The duration mismatch that lets banks earn margin (riding the yield curve) is also what exposes them to runs. The credit-risk reduction depositors enjoy is paid for by the bank's capital. The currency mismatch that funds NOK lending with EUR bonds requires hedging via CCBS — itself exposing the bank to basis-spread movements and counterparty risk.

QAT explains both why banks exist AND why they need regulation.

sections.heading: Brokerage vs Qualitative Asset Transformation
sections.body:
Banks (and other FIs) perform two fundamental functions. The distinction matters because it determines whether the FI carries balance-sheet risk.

**Brokerage.** Bringing transactions in financial claims with complementary needs together — matchmaking. The broker is paid a fee. Critically, the broker bears NO balance-sheet risk: they don't take ownership of the asset, just facilitate the trade. Brokerage resolves PRECONTRACT information asymmetry — adverse selection and duplicated screening. A broker's competitive advantage is **information reusability**: information collected once can be applied across many transactions (cross-sectional and intertemporal).

**Qualitative Asset Transformation (QAT).** Modifying the attributes of financial claims by holding assets that DIFFER from liabilities along one or more dimensions (duration, divisibility, liquidity, credit risk, currency). The mismatch between the asset and liability sides creates inherent risk. The bank earns the spread between asset yield and funding cost as compensation.

**Why the distinction matters.** Brokerage can in principle be performed riskless. QAT cannot — the bank chooses to bear the mismatch risk because the spread compensates for it. The bank can manage this risk three ways: (1) diversify, (2) shift to others via swaps/forwards/options, or (3) passively accept. **If the bank fully shifts all QAT-related risk to a counterparty, the activity reverts to brokerage** — the bank earns a fee, not a spread.

sections.heading: Types of financial intermediaries
sections.body:
Lecture 2 surveys the FI universe. The major types and their distinguishing features:

| Institution | Ownership | Liabilities | Distinguishing feature |
|---|---|---|---|
| Commercial banks | All shareholder-owned | Customer deposits + wholesale | Payment system role; access to central-bank discount window; only FIs that perform monetary policy transmission |
| Thrifts (S&Ls, MSBs) | Mostly mutual | Consumer savings | Specialised in residential mortgages; ownership has historically been mutual (depositors own) |
| Credit unions | Mutual (members) | Consumer deposits | Members must share a 'common bond' (employer, location); regulated by NCUA |
| Investment banks | Stock | Wholesale market funding | Underwriting, M&A, sales/trading; NO monetary services; Chinese walls separate banking from trading |
| Finance companies | Stock | Commercial paper | Lend riskier credits, mostly secured; no deposit insurance, no LOLR access |
| Insurance companies | Mixed | Contingent liabilities | Liabilities triggered by events (death, accident); life-insurance liabilities are very long-duration |
| Pension funds | n/a | Future annuity claims | DC: contributions accumulate; DB: prescribed annuity. Constrained by ERISA |
| Mutual funds | Customer-owned | Open-end (NAV) or closed-end | Open-end shares trade at NAV; closed-end can deviate widely |
| Hedge funds | Limited partnership | Private investment pool | Unlimited fees, riskier strategies, sophisticated-investor only |
| Credit rating agencies | Stock | Subscription / issuer-paid | Brokerage function — process information into ratings; oligopoly: Moody's, S&P, Fitch ~95% |
| Government | Public | Tax-funded | Largest FI in the world (Old Age, Disability, Medicare, housing agencies) |

**Why this matters for exam:** Mid-term papers test knowledge of FI types directly (Feb 2024 P2c on capital vs money markets is one example). T/F questions often hinge on knowing which institution does what — e.g. "investment banks provide monetary services" → FALSE; that is exclusive to commercial banks.

**Goldsmith → fractional-reserve evolution.** Modern banking emerged from goldsmith warehousing: receipts began trading like money, then goldsmiths printed extra receipts to lend. Once liabilities exceeded cash assets, the system became inherently unstable to runs — which is why central-bank LOLR and reserve requirements eventually emerged.

title: Bank Balance Sheets & Accounting
subtitle: Lectures 2 + 3-4 — How banks are structured, how they earn, and how they account for it
examWeight: Core for the MID-TERM (Feb 2024 P1Q1-Q5 was 60 pts of bank-ratio calculation). For the FINAL: provides the underlying framework that IFRS 9 impairment, capital-ratio, and risk-management questions all sit on top of. The HTM/AFS bond-classification distinction was central to the SVB lesson and is testable as a T/F or short-answer.

sections.heading: The bank business model — assets vs liabilities
sections.body:
A bank's balance sheet is an exercise in mismatch. Each line on the asset side is paired with a liability side that differs along at least one of the QAT dimensions:

**Assets (use of funds — typically higher credit risk, longer term, less liquid):**
• Loans to customers (mortgages, business loans, consumer loans)
• Securities and bonds (government, corporate)
• Cash and central-bank deposits
• Interbank claims

**Liabilities (sources of funds — typically lower credit risk, shorter term, more liquid):**
• Customer deposits (retail, corporate)
• Wholesale / market funding (interbank, commercial paper, bonds)
• Subordinated debt
• Equity capital

The gap between asset duration and liability duration is the bank's **maturity transformation**, the source of net interest income — and the source of liquidity, interest-rate, and credit risk simultaneously. Norwegian retail banks' typical structure is roughly 65% deposits + 25% wholesale + 8-10% equity, funding a loan book that's ~80% retail mortgages.

sections.heading: How banks earn money
sections.body:
**Net Interest Income (NII)** is the headline income source: the difference between interest earned on assets and interest paid on liabilities. As a margin: **NIM = NII / Average Total Assets**, typically 0.5–2% for a Norwegian bank.

**"Riding the yield curve."** When the yield curve is upward-sloping (long rates > short rates), the bank funds short and lends long, earning the term premium. The strategy is profitable in normal conditions but exposes the bank to:
• **Interest-rate risk** — a sharp rate rise lowers the value of long bond holdings AND raises funding costs
• **Liquidity risk** — short-term funding can dry up while long-term assets are stuck
• **Yield-curve inversion** — if short rates rise above long rates, the carry turns negative

The SVB collapse (March 2023) is the textbook example of this strategy ending badly.

**Other revenue:**
• Fees and commissions (account fees, payment fees, asset-management fees)
• Trading profits on financial instruments
• Net gains from FX and interest-rate derivatives positions
• Spread on payment services (deposits as a low-cost funding source)

**The leverage effect.** Banks operate with ~5–10% equity (i.e. 10–20× leverage). A thin ROA of ~1% becomes a respectable ROE of ~15% via leverage:

  **ROE = ROA × (Assets / Equity)**

The DuPont decomposition is why bank regulation cares so much about leverage: it amplifies losses just as much as it amplifies returns.

sections.heading: Bond portfolio classification under IFRS 9 — and the SVB lesson
sections.body:
How a bank classifies its bond portfolio matters enormously — same bonds, different classifications, very different reported capital under stress.

**1. Fair Value through P&L (FVtPL).** Mark-to-market every period, gains and losses flow through the income statement. Honest but volatile.

**2. Available for Sale (AFS).** Mark-to-market, but unrealised gains and losses go to **Other Comprehensive Income (OCI)** — they sit in equity rather than P&L. Capital ratios reflect the mark.

**3. Held to Maturity (HTM).** Carried at AMORTISED COST. The fair value is DISCLOSED in notes but does not affect the balance sheet, reported equity, or capital ratios. Permitted only if the bank intends to hold the asset to maturity and has the ability to do so.

**The SVB lesson (March 2023).** SVB held a large long-duration HTM portfolio of US Treasuries and agency MBS. As rates rose 2022–23, the portfolio's fair value fell ~$15.9bn — but because it was HTM, capital ratios looked fine. Concentrated uninsured tech-startup deposits then started withdrawing, forcing SVB to sell HTM assets — at which point losses became realised. Capital evaporated within days. Classification choice has REAL consequences for crisis dynamics: HTM let SVB hide an economic-insolvency that the run then forced into the open.

sections.heading: Money creation in the modern economy
sections.body:
**The textbook story** (incorrect but persistent): banks lend out depositors' money. A reserve-multiplier mechanically scales up deposits.

**The actual mechanism** (Bank of England 2014 Quarterly Bulletin, on the reading list): when a bank makes a loan, it CREATES a matching deposit on its own balance sheet. Both sides of the bank's balance sheet expand simultaneously — the asset is the new loan, the liability is the new deposit credited to the borrower's account. **Loans create deposits, not the other way around.**

**Implications:**
• Reserves are not a binding constraint on lending in modern fiat systems. The binding constraints are **capital** (Basel rules) and **demand** (creditworthy borrowers willing to borrow).
• **Quantitative easing** works by the central bank buying long-dated assets (often from non-banks); the seller's bank gets new reserves; the seller's deposit balance rises; broad money expands. QE directly increases bank deposits.
• Monetary policy operates through interest rates, not reserve quantities — the central bank sets the policy rate, banks adjust their lending rates, lending volumes adjust to the new rate.

This matters for the exam because it reframes what banks ARE: not depositories that lend out savings, but creators of inside money that operates alongside (and is largely interchangeable with) central-bank money.

sections.heading: Key bank ratios — what to compute on the exam
sections.body:
The Mid-term 2024 paper put 60 of 100 points on bank-ratio calculations. Memorise each of these formulas — they show up in T/F questions and direct calculations.

| Ratio | Formula | Typical value |
|---|---|---|
| Deposit-to-loan | Deposits / Loans | 60–100% (Norway) |
| Loan-to-deposit | Loans / Deposits | 100–170% |
| Net Interest Margin | NII / Avg Total Assets | 0.5–2% |
| Cost/Income | Operating expenses / Operating income | 35–50% efficient; >65% poor |
| Return on Assets | Net Income / Avg Total Assets | 0.5–1.5% |
| Return on Equity | Net Income / Avg Equity | 8–15% |
| Equity multiplier | Assets / Equity | 10–20× |
| Non-performing loans | Stage 3 loans / Gross loans | <1% (Nordic) |
| Gross loans | Net loans + Accumulated impairment | (always ≥ Net) |

**Two patterns that have appeared verbatim:**
• **Equity reconciliation** (Feb 2024 P1Q3): Profit retained = Equity_t − Equity_{t-1}. Profit paid out = Profit − retained. Drove the question "why did equity go up by only 20 when profit was 45?"
• **Impairment reconciliation** (Feb 2024 P1Q5): Acc.Impairment_t = Acc.Impairment_{t-1} + new charges − write-offs. Solve for unknown. Then convert write-offs to gross loans written off using the average impairment-coverage rate.

title: Credit Risk & IFRS 9 Impairment
subtitle: Lectures 3–4 — Measurement, provisioning, and balance-sheet implications
examWeight: Core. A numerical question is almost guaranteed on the FINAL. May 2025 Q4 (20 pts: IFRS 9 impairment calc + book-value reconciliation + lifetime-PD reasoning). T/F on credit quality / IFRS 9 features on every paper.

sections.heading: The four parameters
sections.body:
Credit risk is decomposed into four measurable parameters under the Basel/IRB framework:

• **PD** — Probability of Default over a fixed horizon (typically 1 year).
• **LGD** — Loss Given Default; percentage of exposure not recovered after default. Equals 1 − Recovery Rate (after collateral, legal costs).
• **EAD** — Exposure at Default; the amount owed at the moment of default, including accrued interest and undrawn commitments.
• **M** — Maturity of the exposure.

**Expected Loss (covered by provisions):** EL = PD × LGD × EAD

**Unexpected Loss (covered by capital):** the tail risk at 99.9% confidence level over a 1-year horizon. Capital is held to absorb losses that exceed the expected — the regulatory requirement under Basel.

sections.heading: IFRS 9 staging and ECL
sections.body:
IFRS 9 introduced the forward-looking **Expected Credit Loss (ECL)** model, replacing IAS 39's incurred-loss approach. Loans are classified into three stages based on changes in credit quality:

**Stage 1 — performing.** No significant increase in credit risk since origination. Recognise **12-month ECL** (= EAD × PD₁₂ₘ × LGD).

**Stage 2 — significant increase in credit risk (SICR).** Lifetime PD has materially worsened. Recognise **lifetime ECL** (= EAD × PD_lifetime × LGD). Trigger: SICR is measured by changes in PD; collateral changes alone don't trigger Stage 2 — only if they signal higher PD.

**Stage 3 — credit-impaired (default).** Default has occurred. Treat PD = 100%. Recognise **lifetime ECL** = EAD × LGD.

A frequent exam pattern: walk through each stage's impairment formula, calculate book values year-on-year, compute the P&L impact (= change in accumulated impairment).

sections.heading: Standardised vs IRB approaches
sections.body:
**Standardised approach** — regulator-prescribed risk weights based on external ratings. Simple, transparent, but blunt:
• Sovereigns: 0% (typically)
• Banks: 20% (high-rated)
• Retail mortgages: 35%
• Corporate loans: 100% (unrated)

**IRB Foundation** — bank estimates own PD; regulator supplies LGD and EAD.

**IRB Advanced** — bank estimates all four parameters (PD, LGD, EAD, M). Reserved for banks with sophisticated risk-management.

The IRB approach generally produces lower RWA (capital relief) but requires regulatory approval and more disclosure. Norwegian banks heavily use IRB.

sections.heading: Recurring exam patterns
sections.body:
1. **Stage 1/2/3 impairment calculation** (May 2025 Q4): given a table of EAD, PD, LGD per loan, calculate book value year 1 and year 2, the P&L impact, and explain why lifetime PD declines over time.

2. **RWA and capital ratio calculation** (May 2025 Q6a): given a balance sheet with risk weights, compute credit RWA, total REA (adding market and operational risk), and the CET1/T1/total capital ratios.

3. **Bank ratios** (Feb 2024 Q1–5): deposit-to-loan ratio, interest margin on assets, gross loans (= net + accumulated impairment), reconciling impairment movements (write-offs vs new provisions).

4. **T/F traps to watch**: "In IFRS 9 credit quality depends on collateral value" → FALSE (depends on PD); "Reduced impairment increases earnings" → TRUE; "Lower collateral triggers Stage 2 only if it indicates higher PD" → TRUE.

title: Liquidity Risk
subtitle: Lecture 5 (G&T ch. 6) — When solvent banks can still die
examWeight: Core. Mid-term 2024 P2d explicitly tested this (10 pts T/F). Liquidity-risk concepts also underpin May 2025 Q2c (QAT risks), Q1a (derivatives create liquidity risk), and the entire March-2020 NOK turbulence question on Spring 2024 Q4b.

sections.heading: What liquidity risk is — and what it isn't
sections.body:
**Liquidity risk** is the risk that an asset owner cannot realise the asset's value at the moment a sale is desired. The bank is unable to satisfy claims without impairment to its financial or reputational capital.

**The most extreme manifestation** is being unable to sell at any positive price — a market failure that, in credit markets, is called credit rationing.

**Distinguish liquidity from insolvency:**
• **Insolvency** — Liabilities EXCEED Assets at fair value. Net worth is negative. The bank is fundamentally broken.
• **Illiquidity** — Assets exceed liabilities at fair value, but the assets cannot be turned into cash quickly enough to meet current claims. The bank is fundamentally sound but operationally stuck.

The distinction matters because the cure differs:
• Insolvency requires recapitalisation — new equity, bail-in, or government rescue.
• Illiquidity requires liquidity provision — central-bank LOLR is the textbook tool.

**Why information frictions are at the heart of liquidity problems.** When financiers cannot tell a liquidity-stressed bank from an insolvent one, they refuse to fund either. This is exactly the dynamic of every bank run: each individual depositor's optimal action depends on what others do, and uncertainty about the bank's true state becomes self-fulfilling.

sections.heading: Liquidity vs solvency in practice — the LOLR's conundrum
sections.body:
From the OUTSIDE, illiquidity and insolvency look identical: funding dries up, the bank can't meet outflows. But the policy response differs sharply, so the central bank has to make a fast call.

**The financier's perspective vs. the asset's perspective:**
• A liquidity crisis occurs when the bank's FINANCIERS are themselves stretched (their own liquidity stock is low) and can't roll funding — even if the bank's assets are fine.
• An insolvency crisis occurs when the bank's ASSETS have deteriorated, so financiers correctly refuse to fund them.

**In stress, both happen at once.** During 2007–09, repo haircuts on structured products spiked from ~0% to ~50% (Gorton & Metrick's "run on repo"). MMFs faced massive redemptions. Both reflected genuine asset-quality deterioration AND liquidity-channel breakdown.

**Bagehot's Rule (1873)** is the classical answer: lend FREELY, at a PENALTY rate, against GOOD COLLATERAL. The penalty rate ensures only genuinely-illiquid banks borrow (solvent banks find cheaper sources first). Good collateral protects the central bank from absorbing the consequences of insolvency that's been disguised as illiquidity. Three centuries later, central-bank emergency lending still operates on Bagehot's principles.

sections.heading: Three factors determining bank liquidity quality
sections.body:
Greenbaum & Thakor identify three independent dimensions:

**1. Liquidity of the loan portfolio.** Can assets be sold or pledged quickly? Standardised retail mortgages can be securitised; specialised commercial-real-estate loans cannot. The shadow-banking model relied on assuming everything was liquid — until 2008 proved otherwise.

**2. Cash and high-quality liquid assets (HQLA) on hand.** Reserves at the central bank, government securities, top-rated corporate bonds. Not all liquid assets are equally liquid in a stress — MBS were considered liquid until August 2007. Basel III's LCR formalises this: HQLA must satisfy the 30-day stress.

**3. Withdrawal risk in the deposit base.** Diversification of depositors is the most underrated lever. Many small depositors with no concentration → predictable withdrawal flows (Law of Large Numbers). One large institutional deposit at 90% of total funding → very high withdrawal risk. This is exactly why SVB failed: heavily concentrated uninsured tech-startup deposits ran in unison.

**Diversifying withdrawal risk.** As the depositor base grows in number and independence, the withdrawal rate becomes predictable. The fixed-percent cash buffer needed to satisfy any chosen confidence level shrinks. This is why retail-deposit-funded banks are structurally more stable than wholesale-funded ones — the math of large numbers favours retail.

sections.heading: The Lender of Last Resort and its moral hazard
sections.body:
The central bank as LOLR is the keystone that makes fractional-reserve banking viable. Without it, every fractional-reserve bank would be vulnerable to a run that converts illiquidity into insolvency.

**But the LOLR creates its own moral hazard:**
• If LOLR borrowing is cheap and easy, banks hold less voluntary cash. Why hold expensive low-yielding reserves when emergency funding is available?
• Two consequences: (1) deposit **seigniorage** shifts from the public to private banks (banks capture the profit from money creation that would otherwise go to the central bank); (2) the LOLR is exposed to the credit risk of the bank's collateral.

**Reserve requirements as a corrective.** Mandatory reserves prevent banks from offloading their entire liquidity-management problem to the central bank. They restore the appropriate sharing of seigniorage between the public and the banking sector. They also act as a structural backstop independent of LOLR-pricing decisions.

**Pricing the LOLR.** Bagehot's penalty rate is the key. If LOLR borrowing is priced too low, banks treat it as a substitute for their own cash reserves. If priced too high, distressed-but-solvent banks avoid it and fail unnecessarily.

sections.heading: Crisis examples — when liquidity failed
sections.body:
Three case studies the exam treats as common ground:

**Northern Rock (September 2007).** UK mortgage lender, ~75% wholesale-funded. As the ABCP market froze, Northern Rock couldn't roll its funding. The Bank of England's LOLR support became public — and triggered a visible retail run, the first UK bank run since Overend & Gurney (1866). Eventually nationalised. Lesson: even with deposit insurance, depositor confidence can break.

**Repo runs (2007–08).** Gorton & Metrick documented that haircuts on structured-product collateral rose from ~0% to ~50%. Each haircut increase forced borrowers to deleverage; deleveraging meant fire-selling collateral; fire sales pushed prices lower; lower prices justified higher haircuts. A self-reinforcing liquidity spiral that operated outside the deposit-insurance perimeter.

**March 2020 NOK turbulence (Lecture 9 guest lecture).** Norwegian NBFIs (asset managers) had hedged foreign-equity holdings with FX swaps. When equity values fell ~30%, two channels triggered NOK selling: (1) **rebalancing** — over-hedged investors had to buy foreign currency (sell NOK) to honour hedge contracts; (2) **margining** — adverse mark-to-market on FX hedges generated margin calls met by selling Norwegian bonds. Risk premia spiked. Norges Bank intervened progressively (13 March: liquidity + 50bp rate cut → 19 March: FX intervention press release → 7 May: rate to zero).

All three episodes illustrate the same lesson: in modern banking, liquidity risk crosses institutional boundaries. The shadow banks, the FX-swap market, and the regulated-bank perimeter all share the same plumbing — and the same vulnerabilities.

title: Deposit Insurance
subtitle: Lecture 5 — Solving the bank-run problem and the moral hazard it creates
examWeight: Core. FINAL: Final 2023 Q2 (NB Guarantee Fund + super-preference, ~20 pts). MID-TERM: Feb 2025 Q3 (NB Guarantee Fund 20 pts). T/F questions on deposit-insurance moral hazard appear on every paper.

sections.heading: Why deposit insurance exists — the Diamond–Dybvig problem
sections.body:
Banks engage in maturity transformation: short-term deposits funding long-term loans. Diamond & Dybvig (1983) showed this creates two equilibria:

• **Good equilibrium.** Only depositors with genuine early liquidity needs withdraw. The bank holds enough cash to meet them; the rest stay invested.
• **Bad equilibrium (bank run).** Each depositor believes others will withdraw, so they rush to withdraw too. The bank is forced to liquidate long-term assets at fire-sale prices. The run becomes self-fulfilling: the bank fails not because it was insolvent, but because everyone expected it to fail.

**Deposit insurance is the equilibrium-selection mechanism.** By guaranteeing deposits up to a limit, the government removes each depositor's incentive to participate in a run. The bad equilibrium ceases to exist. This was the foundational insight that earned Diamond and Dybvig the 2022 Nobel Prize in Economics.

sections.heading: Coverage: Norway vs the EU
sections.body:
**Norwegian Banks' Guarantee Fund (Bankenes Sikringsfond).** Guarantees deposits up to **NOK 2 million per customer per bank**. Funded by ex-ante contributions from member banks. Coverage is significantly higher than the EU minimum.

**EU/EEA Deposit Guarantee Schemes Directive (DGSD).** Standard coverage of **€100,000 per depositor per bank**. Member-state schemes are pre-funded by levies on member banks.

**Common features:**
• Per-customer limit (not per-account) — a depositor with multiple accounts at the same bank is covered up to the single limit, not multiplied per account.
• Per-bank — if you hold deposits at two separate banks, you're covered up to the limit at each.
• Coverage is automatic — no claim required.
• Speed — payouts target completion within 7 working days under DGSD.

sections.heading: The moral hazard cost
sections.body:
**Deposit insurance creates moral hazard** — and this trade-off is examined on virtually every paper.

• Without insurance, depositors would demand higher rates from risky banks (or move funds to safer ones). This depositor discipline pressures banks to limit risk.
• **With** insurance (within the limit), depositors are insulated from bank-specific risk. They can hunt for the highest deposit rate without monitoring the bank's behaviour.
• The bank can therefore take more risk without paying a higher funding cost. The implicit subsidy is paid for by the insurance fund (and ultimately by the public if the fund is exhausted).

**Mitigants — what regulators do to compensate:**
• **Risk-based premiums.** Member-bank contributions to the fund vary with the bank's risk profile (capital ratios, asset quality). Riskier banks pay more. Partially restores price discipline.
• **Prudential supervision.** Capital requirements (Basel III), liquidity rules (LCR/NSFR), stress testing, and on-site inspections substitute for depositor monitoring.
• **Resolution framework.** BRRD ensures that if a bank does fail, losses are absorbed by shareholders and bondholders before deposit insurance is called on.

The regulatory architecture therefore comes as a package: deposit insurance + risk-based premiums + capital and liquidity rules + resolution framework all interact.

sections.heading: Merton (1977) — deposit insurance as a put option
sections.body:
Merton's analytical framework (on the supplementary reading list) shows why deposit insurance must be priced carefully:

• Treat bank assets as a stochastic process with volatility σ.
• Deposit insurance pays out when assets fall below deposits — i.e., it's economically a **put option** on the bank's assets, struck at the face value of deposits.
• Standard option-pricing logic: the put's value rises with **asset volatility σ** and with **leverage D/A**.

**Implication.** A flat-rate insurance premium (where every bank pays the same percentage of deposits) **underprices risky banks**. Risky banks get an effective subsidy at the expense of safer banks and the insurance fund. This is the analytical basis for risk-based premiums — they restore the option-pricing relationship between premium and underlying risk.

Merton's framework is also why the 1980s S&L crisis happened: deregulation allowed S&Ls to take on more risk; flat-rate FDIC premiums didn't increase to reflect this; the insurance fund absorbed enormous losses.

sections.heading: Super-preference and the Final 2023 question
sections.body:
Under EU and Norwegian law, **covered deposits sit at the very top of the creditor hierarchy** — they are paid out before all other creditors in liquidation or resolution. This "super-preference" protects the deposit-insurance fund itself: when the bank fails, the fund pays out depositors but then steps into the depositors' top-priority position to recover from the bank's estate.

**Final 2023 Q2 asked:** what happens if the deposit-insurance fund's super-preference is removed?

**Consequences:**
• The fund faces higher loss risk on its claim against the failed bank's estate.
• Its capacity to finance "alternative measures" — using fund money to support resolution rather than just paying out depositors — becomes more constrained, since the fund could lose more if it does end up paying out.
• **However**, the fund's discretionary capacity to contribute to alternative measures actually INCREASES, because the cap on its contribution (limited to what it would lose paying out) goes up.
• Depositors outside the guarantee — particularly large corporates with deposits above NOK 2m — see a SIGNIFICANT improvement in their relative ranking (they're no longer behind the super-preferred fund).
• **Funding behaviour shifts.** Large corporates would prefer placing funds as deposits rather than buying senior bonds issued by the bank — deposits now look safer than they did before.

sections.heading: Recurring exam patterns
sections.body:
**T/F traps that appear repeatedly:**
• "Deposit insurance increases moral hazard" → **TRUE** (May 2024 Q1c, Final 2022 Q1d, Mid-term 2024 P2b in negated form)
• "Deposit insurance mitigates moral hazard" → **FALSE** (Mid-term 2024 P2b)

**Essay question structure (20 pts):**
• Define the scheme
• Discuss implications for THREE stakeholder groups: (i) depositors, (ii) banks, (iii) regulators
• Be ready to discuss the super-preference variant

**Key facts to memorise:**
• Norway: NOK 2,000,000 per customer per bank
• EU: €100,000 per depositor per bank
• Funded ex-ante by member-bank contributions
• Risk-based premiums are the standard mitigant for moral hazard
• Super-preference puts covered deposits at the very top of the creditor hierarchy

title: Bank Crises
subtitle: Lecture 6 — From the 1980s S&L crisis to 2008 to 2023
examWeight: Core. FINAL: Spring 2024 Q3 (10 pts — 2008 causes + reforms). T/F questions on the 2008 crisis and its mechanics appear on every paper. Norway's 2008 experience (liquidity not solvency) is a recurring T/F trap.

sections.heading: The 2008 Global Financial Crisis — six causes (Turner Review)
sections.body:
The Spring 2024 Q3 grading guide cites the Turner Review's six causes essentially verbatim. Memorise them:

**1. Macro-imbalances.** China's huge current-account surplus suppressed global real interest rates, prompting a hunt for yield and compressed risk premiums.

**2. Financial innovation and shadow banking.** Securitisation, growth of intra-financial-sector assets and liabilities, increased leverage and maturity transformation in the shadow-banking sector (SIVs, conduits, investment banks at 30–50× leverage, money-market funds).

**3. Misplaced reliance on sophisticated maths.** Rating agencies had little experience rating new complex structured products. Their ratings proved poor predictors of risk and were subject to rapid downgrades when the crisis broke.

**4. Procyclicality and interconnectedness.** When ratings were lowered, repo haircuts widened, derivatives margin requirements rose, institutions hit liquidity problems, fire sales added to the problems, and bank solvency came under pressure. Mark-to-market accounting and VaR risk-management amplified the cycle.

**5. Lack of confidence and transparency.** Opacity about embedded risks dried up money-market funding. Credit froze, leading to economic contraction.

**6. The trigger — US subprime.** Housing prices had risen sharply, underwriting standards weakened, subprime mortgages were securitised globally; when the true risk was revealed, confidence evaporated.

sections.heading: Crisis timeline 2007–2009
sections.body:
Memorise the headline events — they show up in T/F questions, MC questions, and essay context:

• **August 2007.** BNP Paribas suspended redemptions on three ABS funds, citing inability to value assets. Froze European ABCP market overnight. ECB injected €95bn the same day. **Widely regarded as the start of the GFC.**
• **September 2007.** Northern Rock — UK mortgage lender ~75% wholesale-funded — suffered the first UK bank run in over 140 years. Visible queues outside branches AFTER BoE LOLR support became public. Nationalised February 2008.
• **March 2008.** Bear Stearns — run on repo funding; counterparties refused to roll. Fed provided $29bn emergency facility (Section 13(3)); JPMorgan acquired at $10/share.
• **September 15, 2008.** Lehman Brothers files for bankruptcy. $613bn — largest in US history. Triggered global money-market panic; the Reserve Primary Fund "broke the buck" the next day. **The decision NOT to rescue Lehman is widely seen as the worst policy mistake of the crisis.**
• **September 16, 2008.** AIG bailout. AIG Financial Products had sold ~$440bn of CDS protection on structured-credit reference assets. Collateral calls mounted as ratings fell. Fed provided $85bn revolving credit for 79.9% equity stake. Bailout prevented a cascade of CDS losses across global banks.
• **October 2008.** Coordinated government recapitalisations (TARP in the US; equivalent programmes in UK, EU). Fed activated UNLIMITED dollar swap lines with ECB, BoE, BoJ, SNB — the negative dollar basis collapsed within weeks.

sections.heading: Norway's 2008 experience — liquidity, not solvency
sections.body:
A recurring T/F trap (e.g. Spring 2024 Q1a): "The 2008 crisis caused a solvency crisis in the Norwegian banking system." → **FALSE.**

• Norwegian banks were well-capitalised entering 2008 (lessons from the early-90s Norwegian banking crisis had been internalised).
• The 2008 crisis hit Norway through **funding/liquidity** channels, not through asset-side solvency losses.
• Norwegian banks had wholesale funding exposure (especially in foreign currency); when those markets froze, they faced liquidity strain.

**Norges Bank's response:**
• Expanded the collateral framework for liquidity provision.
• **"Golden Card" swap arrangement (Bytteordning).** Banks swapped illiquid covered bonds and mortgages for government T-bills. Restored interbank trust. The cost to taxpayers was minimal because the banks repaid.
• Maintained dollar funding via Fed swap-line access through the ECB.

Result: Norway avoided the worst of the crisis, but the experience drove regulatory tightening (CCyB, systemic-risk buffer, structurally higher capital requirements at DNB).

sections.heading: Post-2008 regulatory reforms
sections.body:
The Spring 2024 Q3b answer lists what to know:

• **Basel III.** Implemented in the EU through CRD/CRR. Stricter capital requirements. Buffer capital requirements. New liquidity and funding requirements (LCR + NSFR). Strengthened supervisory powers and cross-border cooperation.
• **BRRD.** Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive introduced bail-in as the primary tool for failing banks — moves losses from taxpayers to shareholders and creditors.
• **IFRS 9.** New accounting standard for impairment of financial instruments. More forward-looking; earlier recognition of expected credit losses.
• **Activity restrictions.** In the US (Dodd-Frank, Volcker Rule) and UK (Vickers ring-fencing), investment-banking activities were partially separated from retail banking.
• **EMIR / Dodd-Frank derivatives reforms.** Mandatory central clearing of standard derivatives, margin requirements, trade reporting.

Memorise the chain: the cause → the reform. Procyclicality of haircuts/margins → countercyclical buffer + leverage ratio. Off-balance-sheet shadow-banking risk → leverage ratio + LCR + NSFR. Too-big-to-fail → BRRD bail-in + MREL/TLAC. Procyclical loan-loss accounting → IFRS 9.

sections.heading: Earlier crises — Nordic 1988–95, S&L 1980s
sections.body:
**Nordic banking crisis (1988–95).** Norway, Sweden, Finland all suffered banking-sector collapses after deregulation-driven credit booms.

• **Norway (1988–91).** Deregulation (1984–85) → credit boom in property and shipping. Christiania Bank, Fokus Bank, Den norske Bank all needed state recapitalisation. Government took full ownership of the three largest banks; **shareholders were wiped out completely.** Banks were eventually returned to private hands. Swift, decisive resolution.
• **Sweden (1991–93).** Riksbank defended krona peg with 500%+ overnight rates → real-estate collapse. NPLs reached ~11% of GDP. Government issued **blanket guarantee** on all bank liabilities + created **bad banks** (Securum, Retriva) for distressed assets. Template for later crisis management.
• **Finland (1991–95).** Worst of the three. Loss of Soviet export market + fixed exchange rate + post-deregulation credit bubble. Bank losses peaked at ~13% of GDP. Government recapitalised + STS Bank merger.

**1980s US S&L crisis.** Deregulation + flat-rate deposit insurance (Merton trap) + high interest rates → S&Ls became insolvent on a mark-to-market basis but kept open via regulatory forbearance. ~1,000 institutions eventually failed. Direct cost to taxpayers: ~$124bn (FDIC, 1988 history).

sections.heading: Recent crises — SVB, Credit Suisse, Norwegian intervention (2022–23)
sections.body:
**Silicon Valley Bank (March 2023).** Long-duration HTM Treasury and MBS portfolio + concentrated uninsured tech-startup deposits. Rising rates → ~$15.9bn unrealised losses on HTM book (DISCLOSED only, not in capital ratios). Failed asset sales triggered loss recognition; social-media-driven run forced regulatory takeover. FDIC invoked the Systemic Risk Exception to guarantee uninsured deposits. Fed launched the BTFP emergency facility.

**Credit Suisse (March 2023).** Years of governance failures and risk-management scandals. Forced merger with UBS by Swiss authorities, with CHF 100bn central-bank liquidity + CHF 9bn loss guarantee. **Controversially, ~CHF 16bn of AT1 hybrid capital was written down to zero while equity holders received UBS shares** — under the terms of the Swiss AT1 contracts but contrary to the standard creditor hierarchy. Repriced AT1 markets globally.

**Sberbank Europe (March 2022).** Sanctions-driven deposit flight after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Single Resolution Board acted within days using the sale-of-business tool — subsidiaries transferred to local banks, parent wound up.

**Næringsbanken (Norway 2022–23).** Pre-emptive intervention by Finanstilsynet — loan freeze, P2R increase, forced recapitalisation. Resolution avoided through early action.

sections.heading: Bernanke (1983) — non-monetary effects
sections.body:
Bernanke's 1983 paper, motivating his share of the 2022 Nobel Prize, argues that bank failures during the Great Depression had **non-monetary** real-economy effects beyond Friedman & Schwartz's monetary-contraction story.

**Mechanism:** When banks fail, intermediation services are destroyed. Borrowers — especially small businesses with no public-debt-market access — lose their relationship lenders. Information capital built up over years is wiped out. Even with the same money supply, credit allocation collapses.

**Implication for 2008+:** This is why Lehman's failure triggered such severe real-economy damage. Ivashina & Scharfstein (2010) document the bank-lending contraction empirically: banks reliant on Lehman as a counterparty cut new lending sharply, regardless of borrower quality.

**Implication for policy:** It justifies aggressive central-bank intervention to prevent bank failures, even if doing so creates moral hazard. The cost of letting a systemic bank fail isn't just the depositors who lose money — it's the credit network that takes years to rebuild.

title: Basel Regulation & Capital Requirements
subtitle: Lecture 7 — Three types of capital requirements and the buffer stack
examWeight: Core. Capital ratio calculations on May 2025 Q6 (3 pts), recurring T/F questions on every paper.

sections.heading: Evolution: Basel I → Basel II → Basel III
sections.body:
**Basel I (1988).** Simple flat 8% capital ratio with crude risk weights:
• Sovereigns: 0% (typically)
• Banks: 20% (high-rated)
• Mortgages: 50%
• Corporate loans: 100% (unrated)

Credited with stabilising international banking through the 1990s. Criticised for being risk-insensitive — a 100% weight on every corporate loan ignores the difference between AAA and CCC.

**Basel II (2004).** Three pillars: (1) minimum capital with IRB models, (2) supervisory review, (3) market discipline. Added operational risk to the capital denominator. Allowed banks to use INTERNAL RATINGS-BASED (IRB) models — Foundation (bank estimates PD) or Advanced (bank estimates all parameters). Criticised for procyclicality — risk weights fall in booms (the period of greatest exuberance) and rise in busts (when banks most need lower requirements).

**Basel III (2010–17, ongoing as CRR3 / CRD VI from 2025).** Post-2008 overhaul:
• Stricter capital QUALITY — focus on CET1 (raised from 2% under Basel II to 4.5% under Basel III)
• **Buffer stack** on top of Pillar 1 minimums (conservation, countercyclical, systemic risk, O-SII, G-SIB)
• Non-risk-sensitive **leverage ratio** (3% of Tier 1 / total exposures) as a backstop against RWA gaming
• Liquidity rules: **LCR** (30-day stress) and **NSFR** (1-year sustainable funding)
• **MREL / TLAC** for bail-in capacity
• Implemented in the EU through the Capital Requirements Directive (CRD) and Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR); CRR3 / CRD VI are the latest updates rolling out from 2025

Memorise the chain: each Basel III innovation maps to a specific 2008-crisis failure. Off-balance-sheet shadow banking → leverage ratio + LCR + NSFR. Procyclical haircuts/margins → countercyclical buffer. Too-big-to-fail → MREL + bail-in framework. Procyclical loan-loss accounting → IFRS 9.

sections.heading: The three types of capital requirements
sections.body:
Basel III imposes three distinct types of requirement, each addressing a different concern:

**1. Risk-sensitive (capital adequacy ratio):**
  Capital adequacy = Own Funds / RWA

This is the headline ratio. Own funds are weighted by the risk of each asset.

**2. Non-risk-sensitive (leverage ratio):**
  Leverage ratio = Tier 1 / Total Exposures

A simple backstop. Doesn't depend on risk weights, so it is robust to RWA gaming or model failure. The Basel III minimum is 3%.

**3. Bail-in capital (MREL):**
  MREL = (Own Funds + Eligible Liabilities) / RWA

Ensures enough "bail-in-able" liabilities exist before a crisis to absorb losses and recapitalise without taxpayer cost. The Loss Absorption Amount + Recapitalisation Amount.

sections.heading: Own funds hierarchy (quality matters)
sections.body:
Capital is not all equal. Quality is graded:

• **CET1 (Common Equity Tier 1)** — common equity less deductions (goodwill, proposed dividends, intangibles). Highest quality.
• **AT1 (Additional Tier 1)** — perpetual hybrid capital. Convertible to equity or written down on a going-concern basis (i.e. while the bank is still operating). Coupon payments at the bank's discretion.
• **T2 (Tier 2)** — subordinated debt. Only written down in resolution or liquidation (gone-concern).

Minimums:
• CET1 minimum: 4.5% of RWA
• AT1 minimum: 1.5% (or fill with CET1)
• T2 minimum: 2.0% (or fill with CET1 or AT1)
• **Pillar 1 minimum total: 8%**

sections.heading: The Basel III buffer stack — DNB example end-2025
sections.body:
On top of Pillar 1 minimums, banks must maintain capital buffers:

| Component | % of RWA |
|---|---|
| CET1 minimum | 4.5% |
| AT1 minimum | 1.5% |
| T2 minimum | 2.0% |
| **Pillar 1 minimum** | **8.0%** |
| Pillar 2 Requirement (P2R, bank-specific) | 1.7% |
| Conservation buffer (CET1) | 2.5% |
| Countercyclical buffer (CET1) | 2.5% |
| Systemic risk buffer (CET1) | 4.5% |
| O-SII buffer (CET1) | 2.0% |
| Pillar 2 Guidance (P2G) | 1.0% |
| **Total CET1 requirement** | **~18%** |
| **Total capital requirement** | **~22%** |

This stack is BIG — far above the headline 4.5% CET1 minimum. The buffers exist to be drawn down in stress without forcing immediate corrective action.

sections.heading: Liquidity requirements (Basel III post-2010)
sections.body:
**LCR (Liquidity Coverage Ratio):** 
  HQLA / Net cash outflow over 30-day stress ≥ 100%

Ensures the bank can survive a 30-day run scenario with high-quality liquid assets alone.

**NSFR (Net Stable Funding Ratio):**
  Available Stable Funding / Required Stable Funding (1-year) ≥ 100%

Ensures the funding structure is sustainable over a longer horizon — not just a 30-day window.

sections.heading: Calculating capital ratios — the standard exam pattern
sections.body:
**Step 1: Calculate Credit RWA.** Sum each asset × its risk weight.

**Step 2: Add market-risk REA + operational-risk REA.** These are usually given.

**Step 3: Compute own funds.**
• CET1 = Equity − deductions (often given as nil)
• T1 = CET1 + AT1 (hybrid capital)
• Total = T1 + T2 (subordinated debt)

**Step 4: Divide.**
• CET1 ratio = CET1 / Total REA
• T1 ratio = T1 / Total REA
• Total capital ratio = Total Capital / Total REA

Worked example (May 2025 Q6a, Lilledal Savingsbank):
• Credit RWA: 10×0 + 40×0 + 500×0.35 + 400×1.0 + 30×1.0 = 605
• Total REA: 605 + 15 (market) + 75 (op) = 695
• CET1 ratio = 100/695 = 14.4% ✓

title: FX Swaps, CCBS & Covered Interest Parity
subtitle: Lecture 8 + Olav Syrstad's note — Pricing and hedging foreign-currency exposure
examWeight: Important. FX-swap pricing calculations on Spring 2024 Q4a and Final 2022 Q3a; March-2020 NOK-weakening question on Spring 2024 Q4b. Highly likely on May 2026.

sections.heading: FX Swap mechanics
sections.body:
An **FX swap** is a simultaneous agreement to exchange two currencies at today's spot rate, and to reverse the exchange at a pre-agreed forward rate at a specified future date. Two legs:

• **Near leg:** exchange of currencies at spot S₀ today.
• **Far leg:** re-exchange at forward rate F at maturity.

Because F is locked at inception, neither party bears FX risk over the swap's life. The instrument is economically equivalent to a **collateralised loan**: one currency is pledged as collateral to borrow the other.

sections.heading: Covered Interest Parity (CIP)
sections.body:
The forward rate is determined by a no-arbitrage condition known as Covered Interest Rate Parity:

  **F = S₀ × (1 + r_quote × t) / (1 + r_base × t)**

where t is the tenor in years, r_quote is the interest rate of the quoted (numerator) currency, and r_base is the rate of the base (denominator) currency.

**Intuition.** If the quote currency has a higher interest rate, the forward rate must be HIGHER (more units of quote currency per base at maturity) — equivalently, the higher-yielding currency depreciates forward and the lower-yielding currency appreciates forward. This compensates the party who LENDS the LOW-yielding currency: they hand it over at spot and get back more of the high-yielding currency at maturity, exactly offsetting the interest they forwent. Without this adjustment, riskless arbitrage would be possible (borrow low-yield currency, swap to high-yield, deposit, swap back).

**Swap points** = F − S₀ = the compensation embedded in the exchange rate for the interest-rate differential. Positive when the quote currency has a higher rate.

sections.heading: Worked example — DKK/NOK 6-month FX swap
sections.body:
(From May 2024 Q4a and Final 2022 Q3a — same numbers)

Given: S₀ = 1.65 NOK/DKK, r_NOK = 4% p.a., r_DKK = 2% p.a., tenor = 6 months.

**Step 1.** F = 1.65 × (1 + 0.04 × 0.5) / (1 + 0.02 × 0.5) = 1.65 × 1.02/1.01 = **1.67 NOK/DKK**.

**Step 2.** Swap points = F − S₀ = 1.67 − 1.65 = **0.02 = 2 points (200 pips)**.

Intuition: NOK has the higher rate, so DKK appreciates forward (1 DKK is worth more NOK forward than at spot). This compensates the DKK lender — they hand over 1 DKK at spot and receive more NOK back at maturity, exactly offsetting the lower DKK interest they earn during the swap.

sections.heading: Cross-Currency Basis Swap (CCBS)
sections.body:
A **CCBS** is a long-dated instrument (typically 1 to 30 years) used to convert long-term funding from one currency to another:

• **Initial exchange** of principal at the **spot rate**.
• Throughout the swap, **floating-rate payments** in each currency are exchanged.
• **Final re-exchange** of principal at the **same spot rate** as inception (NOT a forward rate).

Critical distinction from FX swaps: in a CCBS, the principal re-exchange happens at the original spot rate, not at a forward rate. The interest-rate differential is handled through the **floating coupon legs**, not embedded in a forward rate.

**Basis spread.** In theory the basis = 0 (CIP). In practice, a spread is added to one leg (typically the non-USD leg). The spread reflects counterparty credit risk, supply/demand imbalances, and capital constraints. It widened sharply in 2008 (USD scarce) and 2020.

sections.heading: Full hedge example — EUR bond → NOK floating
sections.body:
**Scenario.** A Norwegian mortgage company issues a 5-year EUR-denominated covered bond at 3.50% fixed coupon, EUR 100m. The proceeds fund NOK adjustable-rate mortgages earning NIBOR 3M + 80 bps.

**Two risks to hedge:** (i) FX (EUR liabilities, NOK assets); (ii) interest-rate (fixed coupon, floating asset income).

**Step 1: Issue EUR bond.** Pay EUR 3.50% fixed coupon to investors.

**Step 2: EUR IRS** — receive fixed 3.50%, pay EURIBOR 3M. Cancels the bond coupon, leaves a EURIBOR 3M obligation.

**Step 3: EUR/NOK CCBS** — receive EURIBOR 3M (cancels IRS pay-leg), pay NIBOR 3M − basis. Initial principal exchange at spot 11.50 NOK/EUR. Re-exchange at the SAME 11.50 at maturity.

**Net position:** NIBOR 3M + 80 bps − basis. **Clean floating NOK margin**, all FX and interest-rate risk hedged.

**Residual risks:** basis-spread movements, counterparty credit risk on swaps, rollover/refinancing risk.

sections.heading: March 2020 — over-hedging and NOK weakening
sections.body:
(Spring 2024 Q4b, Final 2022 Q3b — recurring exam question)

During the COVID shock, foreign equity portfolios held by Norwegian NBFIs lost ~30% of value. Investors had hedged the foreign-currency exposure with FX swaps sized to the original portfolio value.

**The over-hedge mechanic:**
• Foreign asset value falls in foreign currency terms.
• Hedge is now LARGER than the underlying exposure (over-hedged).
• To honour the hedge contracts (which require delivering the original notional of foreign currency), investors must BUY additional foreign currency.
• That means SELLING NOK in the spot market.

**The margining mechanic (parallel channel):**
• NOK depreciates → mark-to-market on FX hedges turns against short-NOK positions → margin calls.
• To meet margin calls, NBFIs sell Norwegian bonds → bond prices fall → risk premiums spike.

Both mechanisms drove the unprecedented NOK depreciation observed 16–20 March 2020. Norges Bank intervened: 13 March extra liquidity + 50bp rate cut; 18 March collateral changes; 19 March possible-FX-intervention press release; 20 March 75bp rate cut to 0.25%; 7 May rate cut to zero.

title: Securitisation & Structured Finance
subtitle: Lecture 10 — From originate-to-distribute to the GFC and back
examWeight: Core. T/F questions on synthetic vs. traditional appear every year.

sections.heading: Two models of bank lending
sections.body:
**Traditional model:** Deposit → Loan → Hold to maturity. The bank originates, holds, and bears the credit risk on the loan to maturity. Has skin in the game throughout.

**Securitised model:** Originate → Pool → Tranche → Sell. The bank originates loans, pools them into a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV), the SPV issues tranches of bonds backed by the pool, and the bonds are sold to investors. The bank no longer holds the credit risk.

This shift has profound consequences. The bank's incentive to screen carefully is weakened (it doesn't bear the loss). The bank's funding need is removed. The risk migrates to capital-market investors.

sections.heading: Tranching and credit enhancement
sections.body:
An SPV holds a loan pool. Cash flows from the pool are paid out in **waterfall** sequence to different tranches:

• **Senior tranche** (rated AAA) — paid first, lowest yield.
• **Mezzanine tranches** (BBB / BB) — paid next.
• **Equity / first-loss tranche** — paid last, absorbs first losses, highest yield.

**Credit enhancement** mechanisms protect senior tranches:
• **Subordination** — junior tranches absorb losses first.
• **Overcollateralisation** — pool value > tranche notionals.
• **External guarantees / monoline insurance** (pre-GFC).
• **Reserve accounts** capturing excess spread.

sections.heading: Synthetic vs traditional — the critical distinction
sections.body:
**Traditional (true-sale) securitisation:** Loans are LEGALLY SOLD to the SPV. They leave the bank's balance sheet entirely. Two effects:
• **Funding** — the bank gets cash and no longer needs to fund the loans.
• **Capital relief** — RWA falls because the credit risk has left.

**Synthetic securitisation:** The loans STAY on the bank's balance sheet. Credit risk is transferred to investors via CDS or financial guarantees on a reference pool. One effect:
• **Capital relief** — RWA falls because credit risk is transferred.
• **No funding** — the bank still funds the loans.

**The exam-trap:** "Synthetic securitisation provides funding" → FALSE. "Synthetic securitisation reduces capital requirements" → TRUE. "CDS plays a role in synthetic securitisation" → TRUE (it's the credit-risk-transfer instrument).

sections.heading: Why securitisation broke in the GFC
sections.body:
**1. Originate-to-distribute weakened screening.** With no skin in the game, originators (especially mortgage brokers) had reduced incentive to verify borrower quality. NINJA loans (No Income, No Job, No Assets) proliferated.

**2. Opacity of CDOs.** Pooled portfolios of MBS, then CDOs of CDO tranches (CDO²), made it impossible for investors to understand the underlying credit. Trust collapsed when subprime defaulted.

**3. Rating-agency failures.** Issuer-pays model created conflicts of interest. Models relied on historical correlations from a benign housing-price period; correlations spiked in stress, and AAA tranches defaulted.

**4. Procyclical haircuts and margins.** When ratings were downgraded, repo haircuts widened, margin requirements rose, derivatives counterparties demanded collateral. Forced fire sales spiralled.

**5. Shadow banking maturity mismatch.** SIVs and ABCP conduits funded long-dated MBS/CDOs with short-term ABCP. When the ABCP market froze on 9 August 2007 (BNP Paribas suspended redemptions on three funds), conduits couldn't roll funding. Sponsors had to absorb them back onto their balance sheets — bringing the off-balance-sheet risk back home.

title: Bank Recovery & Resolution
subtitle: Lecture 11 — BRRD, bail-in, creditor hierarchy, and MREL
examWeight: Core. Featured on every recent FINAL paper as a 15-pt essay+calculation block (May 2025 Q6, May 2024 Q6, Final 2023 Q5, Final 2022 Q4). May 2025 Q6 included a capital-ratio + bail-in waterfall calculation.

sections.heading: BRRD — three phases of bank life
sections.body:
The EU's **Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive** organises bank stress management into three phases:

**1. Normal phase.** Financial optimisation, indicators "green," no special action.

**2. Recovery phase.** Bank-led — the bank activates its **Recovery Plan** (drawn up by the bank, approved by the supervisor). Measures may include suspending dividends, raising capital, divesting assets, restructuring. The aim is to restore the bank to normal under its own steam.

**3. Resolution phase.** Authority-led — when the bank is **"failing or likely to fail" (FOLF)** AND it is in the public interest to refinance/restructure rather than liquidate. The resolution authority (in Norway: Finanstilsynet) executes the **Resolution Plan**.

If resolution is not in the public interest, the alternative is **liquidation** (ordinary insolvency proceedings).

sections.heading: FOLF triggers — four conditions
sections.body:
A bank is "failing or likely to fail" if any of these is true:

1. **No longer meets authorisation requirements** — particularly solvency or liquidity.
2. **Liabilities exceed assets** (balance-sheet insolvency).
3. **Unable to pay debts as they fall due** (cash-flow insolvency).
4. **Requires extraordinary public financial support.**

Any one of these can trigger resolution. Most failures combine several.

sections.heading: The four resolution tools
sections.body:
Once a bank is in resolution, the authority can use one or more of:

**1. Bail-in** — write down equity and convert subordinated debt into new equity, recapitalising the bank without external funds. The default tool for systemic banks.

**2. Sale of business** — transfer all or part of the failing bank to a willing private buyer. Used in Sberbank Europe (2022): subsidiaries transferred quickly, parent wound up.

**3. Bridge institution** — temporary public entity that holds the failing bank's assets and operations while a permanent solution (sale or liquidation) is arranged. Preserves critical functions.

**4. Asset separation** — "bad bank" / asset management vehicle holds toxic assets while the "good bank" continues operating. Used during 1990s Nordic crises (Securum in Sweden).

sections.heading: Bail-in — the creditor hierarchy waterfall
sections.body:
Losses are absorbed **bottom-up** through the creditor hierarchy:

1. **Equity** — wiped out first.
2. **AT1 hybrid capital** — written down or converted to equity.
3. **Tier 2 subordinated debt** — written down or converted.
4. **Senior non-preferred bonds** — converted next (these instruments exist explicitly to be bail-in-able).
5. **Senior unsecured bonds** — converted only if needed.
6. **Deposits** — covered deposits absorb last; uninsured deposits before covered.

**Worked example (May 2025 Q6).** Lilledal Savingsbank: equity reduced to 20, total REA 700, target CET1 12% → needed CET1 = 84.

• Old equity (CET1) ............... 20
• Convert AT1 hybrid capital ...... 10
• Convert T2 subordinated debt ... 20
• Convert non-preferred senior ... 34
• ──────────────────────────────
• **Total CET1 = 84** ✓

Note: only 34 of the 100 non-preferred senior bonds were converted — bail-in stops as soon as the target is met. Senior unsecured and deposits were not touched.

sections.heading: MREL and the implicit subsidy
sections.body:
**MREL** (Minimum Requirement for own funds and Eligible Liabilities) ensures that enough bail-in-able liabilities exist BEFORE a crisis to absorb losses without taxpayer cost.

  MREL = (Own Funds + Eligible Liabilities) / RWA

MREL has two components:
• **Loss Absorption Amount (LAA)** — to absorb losses on the way down (typically equal to current capital requirement).
• **Recapitalisation Amount (RA)** — to rebuild capital to operating levels post-resolution.

**Why this matters: the "too big to fail" problem.** Pre-2008, large banks enjoyed an **implicit government guarantee**: markets believed governments would bail out systemic banks rather than impose losses on senior creditors. This subsidised funding for big banks (lower spreads), distorted competition, and incentivised excess size and risk.

**Bail-in as remedy:**
• No taxpayer money — losses are absorbed inside the bank.
• Markets price in bail-in risk → the implicit subsidy disappears → big banks face their true cost of risk.
• Creditors and management have skin in the game.

MREL ensures bail-in is operationally possible. Without enough bail-in-able liabilities, bail-in cannot work — and the temptation to bail out returns.

sections.heading: Recent applications
sections.body:
**SVB (March 2023)** — not a strict BRRD case (US regulation), but illustrates the same dynamics. HTM bond losses + concentrated uninsured deposits triggered a social-media-driven run. FDIC invoked the Systemic Risk Exception to guarantee uninsured deposits.

**Credit Suisse (March 2023)** — Swiss authorities forced merger with UBS, providing CHF 100bn liquidity and a CHF 9bn loss guarantee. Controversially, AT1 was written down BEFORE equity (a legal but commercially shocking outcome) — equity holders received UBS shares. Caused a sharp repricing of the AT1 market globally.

**Sberbank Europe (2022)** — sanctions-driven deposit flight; SRB decision within days. Subsidiaries transferred (sale of business tool); parent wound up.

**Næringsbanken, Norway (2022–23)** — pre-emptive intervention: loan freeze, P2R increase, forced recapitalisation. Resolution avoided through early action.

title: ESG Risks & Climate
subtitle: DNB guest lecture — Environmental, Social, Governance integration in banking
examWeight: Important. New on the syllabus, appeared first on May 2025 Q5 (15 pts). High probability for May 2026.

sections.heading: What ESG covers
sections.body:
ESG risk is a **transversal driver** of credit, market, operational, and reputational risk — not a separate risk category. The EBA expects banks to integrate ESG into risk appetite, governance, internal controls, risk assessment, and reporting.

**Environmental:** climate change, resource depletion, pollution, biodiversity.
**Social:** labour practices, community impact, consumer protection, diversity.
**Governance:** board composition, executive compensation, corruption, shareholder rights, risk culture.

sections.heading: Environmental risk — two buckets
sections.body:
**1. Physical risks**

• **Acute** — extreme weather: hurricanes, floods, wildfires. Direct losses if borrowers/collateral are impacted (insurance claims, defaulted property loans, business-interruption losses).
• **Chronic** — long-term shifts: rising sea levels, changing precipitation, drought. Affects asset valuation over time. FIs may find some regions become less viable for lending (declining property values, rising NPLs).

**2. Transition risks**

• **Political and legal (regulatory)** — carbon pricing, emissions caps, mandatory disclosure (TCFD, CSRD). Borrowers in fossil-fuel-intensive industries face higher compliance costs and may default.
• **Market** — shifts toward low-carbon technologies leave incumbents with stranded assets. Investor divestment hits share prices and credit spreads.
• **Reputational** — lending to harmful sectors damages brand, attracts activist or regulatory pressure.

sections.heading: Social and governance risks
sections.body:
**Social:**
• **Labour practices** — fair wages, working conditions, labour rights, diversity & inclusion.
• **Community impact** — displacement, public health, infrastructure burden. Example: a mining company infringing on local water supply provoking outrage and operational disruption.
• **Consumer protection** — product safety, data privacy, ethical marketing. Failures invite lawsuits and regulatory scrutiny.

**Governance:**
• **Board composition / independence** — diversity and skill matter; lack of either increases groupthink risk.
• **Corruption / bribery** — legal liability, reputational damage, financial loss.
• **Shareholder rights** — fair treatment, executive compensation, transparency.
• **Risk culture** — central to the failure of Credit Suisse 2023; weak controls and tone-at-the-top led to scandal accumulation and ultimately collapse.

sections.heading: Bank-level integration (DNB practitioner view)
sections.body:
DNB's framework — directly from Martin Andersen's guest lecture:

• **Multi-layer protective barriers** mirror the BRRD recovery/resolution architecture: normal operating phase → recovery phase → resolution phase, with capital, liquidity, and other indicators monitored at each.
• **Risk-appetite integration** — climate transmission channels are explicitly built into risk-appetite statements.
• **Climate scenario analysis** — DNB participates in UNEP FI / TCFD analyses to understand portfolio sensitivity under different climate scenarios.
• **Sustainability targets** — net-zero emissions by 2050; reduce financed-emissions intensity by 2030 (oil and gas −25%, shipping −33%, commercial property −25–35%); commit NOK 1500bn to sustainable transition by 2030.
• **Reporting** — Integrated Reporting framework, GRI compliance, SASB materiality assessment, TCFD/CDP-aligned climate reporting.

**Regulatory pressures:**
• EBA Guidelines on ESG Risk Management.
• Green Infrastructure Supporting Factor (25% capital relief on qualifying green exposures).
• Banks without sufficient climate-risk management may face capital add-ons or fines under CRD VI/CRR3.
• CSRD requires credible transition plans where material risks are identified (double-materiality assessment).
